title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Utica prolongs its data center moratorium today amid rising local fights over power, water and noise.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we start with Utica's city council voting to extend its existing moratorium on data centers, keeping large projects out of this Macomb County city for now.
That's the big one today, Graham. Why does this extension matter so much right now?
It shields residents from sudden spikes in demand on local power and water systems. No immediate tax shifts or infrastructure strain from hyperscale facilities.
How long has Utica had this ban in place already?
They've had a moratorium running, and today's vote simply prolongs it. It's part of a pattern we've seen in several places this week.
What are the bigger stakes here for electric bills and water use?
Data centers can pull hundreds of megawatts and millions of gallons of water. When that hits the grid, utilities often pass costs to all ratepayers through higher bills or new lines.
Who are the main players pushing these projects versus the communities resisting?
Tech firms and utilities see the economic upside, while townships and residents worry about farmland loss, noise, and strained services. Local officials are caught in the middle.
Has this kind of moratorium wave happened before in Michigan?
We've seen similar pauses in places like Chippewa County yesterday and Garfield Township on Friday. Communities are buying time to study impacts before locking anything in.
What happens next for Utica specifically?
The extension keeps the door closed for now. Officials can use the time to write clearer rules on power, water, and zoning if interest picks up again.
How does this connect to the noise complaints we're hearing elsewhere today?
Exactly the quality-of-life angle. In Dowagiac, neighbors are suing over a nonstop hum that sounds like a vacuum running 24/7, and the company is already offering buyouts after fines.
That's in today's news too. What about St. Clair County?
Residents there are weighing the same trade-off: promised jobs and tax revenue against constant humming that disrupts daily life. It's the eastern Michigan version of the debate.
So the Utica move feels like a signal to other towns?
It does. It shows residents can push back and protect capacity without rushing into big projects that might raise everyone's bills.
What about the broader pattern across rural counties?
Interest is growing, but places like Calhoun County are also debating year-long halts over jobs versus power strain. The pause would delay projects drawing serious megawatts and water.
Any sense of how many townships have hit pause so far?
It's spreading. We had Garfield Township freeze new builds after a sloppy filing on Friday, and Augusta Township is nearing a vote on rules for a big Oracle-scale proposal.
That Augusta one ties into DTE territory, right?
Yes, same service area as Saline. The outcome will show how much new load hits ratepayers and whether the township gets meaningful revenue.
Speaking of DTE, their earnings preview this week highlighted data centers as a profit driver.
That's the flip side. Growth there often means more demand on the grid, which can translate into higher rates or infrastructure costs passed to households.
Indiana Michigan Power took a different step on Saturday though.
They pledged to shield residential customers from footing the bill for new data center power lines. Consumer groups are watching how that holds up in rate cases.
And the Senate candidates split on this over the weekend too.

Democratic primary contenders laid out different plans for regulating demand and protecting ratepayers from transmission costs. Some want utilities or tech firms to cover upgrades; others would spread costs across all customers.
That gives primary voters a clear difference on something that hits monthly bills.
It does. The issue is moving from abstract to concrete for a lot of people.
Back to Utica for a second — does extending the ban change anything for nearby Macomb County residents?
It keeps the status quo. No sudden tax shifts or infrastructure strain tied to hyperscale facilities, at least for the extended period.
What if other towns follow suit?
Development pressure could shift to places without pauses, or stall overall while communities study land, power, and service impacts.
Any early signs that's already happening?
Chippewa County is weighing its own temporary moratorium in the eastern Upper Peninsula. Residents there could see proposals stall depending on the outcome.
So the Utica vote is part of a bigger conversation about how much industrial growth communities will accept.
Precisely. The balance between economic gains and quality-of-life hits like noise, water use, and higher bills.
What should listeners watch for in the coming weeks?
More township meetings on zoning and tax terms, plus how utilities handle the cost-shifting debate in rate cases.
Let's move to quick hits on the rest of today's news.
Dowagiac residents are pushing a lawsuit over data center noise, saying the constant hum violates local rules. The company has been fined and is now offering to buy affected homes.
That sounds like a preview of what could hit other neighborhoods if sound limits stay weak.
St. Clair County is facing the same tension — noise complaints versus promised jobs and tax revenue.
Local officials there are under pressure to decide how much industrial growth is worth the daily disruption.
Yesterday Chippewa County leaders started weighing a temporary freeze on new proposals while they study land and power impacts.
That could stall development pressure in the eastern Upper Peninsula.
On Saturday the Indiana Michigan Power pledge came out, promising residential customers won't pay for new data center lines.
And Senate candidates split on whether to let data centers drive up power bills or force tech firms and utilities to cover upgrades.

Friday brought several more pauses: Garfield Township after an incomplete application, Calhoun County debating a year-long halt over jobs and electricity strain, and Augusta Township nearing a vote on rules for a large proposal.
DTE's Q2 preview also flagged data-center growth as a key earnings driver, which often means more costs passed to households.
No major public meetings on the calendar for tonight or tomorrow that we've confirmed yet.
Listeners can keep an eye on township agendas for updates on zoning and moratorium votes.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Utica Extends Ban as Michigan Communities Push Back on Data Center Strain
